title: Desire, gently
hook: for now, don't desire what isn't up to you; only choose and refuse lightly (Enchiridion 2)

segments.voice: Yesterday: George Long's translation, what is ours, the two piles. Your line was start here. When you got stuck, did you ask whether it was in your power? Day three hundred thirty-four.

Every want comes with a promise tucked inside it. Want the job, and the want quietly promises: you'll get it. Dread the diagnosis, and the dread promises: you'll escape it. The promise is easy to miss until it breaks, and then the disappointment can seem like something done to us. Section two of the handbook takes those promises seriously. It doesn't tell a beginner to stop wanting forever. It says something gentler, and odder, with two small words that matter a lot: for now. Today: desire, gently.
screen: `EVERY WANT HIDES A PROMISE.` → `THE PROMISE BREAKS.` → `FOR NOW.`

segments.voice: First, the two promises. Desire, Epictetus says, promises that you'll get what you desire. Aversion promises that you won't fall into what you avoid. Miss what you desire and you feel unlucky. Fall into what you avoid and you feel wretched. Second, move aversion home. If you only push away things in your own power, like your own cruelty or cowardice, you'll never fall into them against your will. But try to avoid sickness, death or poverty, and you've signed up for misery, because those aren't yours to avoid. So he says: take aversion off everything outside your power, and set it on the things inside it. Third, desire, for now. Here the handbook surprises people. For the present, he says, set desire aside completely. If you desire what isn't up to you, he says, you're bound to be disappointed. And the good things that are up to you, a steady character, sound judgment, aren't yet within a beginner's reach. This is advice for someone starting out, not a rule for a whole life. Fourth, choose lightly. Meanwhile, use only choosing and refusing, moving toward a thing or away from it, and do even that lightly, without straining, with a reservation. The Stoics meant a quiet clause attached to a plan. Seneca gives one: I'll sail, unless something gets in the way. Neighbors say something close. Muslims say in sha Allah, if God wills, and the letter of James in the New Testament says to speak of plans with: if the Lord will. Epictetus' version is simply: lightly, and for now.
screen: `DESIRE AND AVERSION MAKE PROMISES.` · `AVOID ONLY WHAT IS YOURS TO AVOID.` · `FOR NOW, SET DESIRE DOWN.` · `CHOOSE LIGHTLY, WITH A RESERVATION.` · then, large: `GENTLY, FOR NOW.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one thing you want right now that isn't fully up to you. A reply, a result, a yes from someone. Feel the want in your body: where does it pull? Now, without pushing it away, add the quiet clause. I'd like this, if nothing prevents it. Say it inside, once or twice. Notice whether your grip loosens even a little. You're still allowed to want it. You're just holding it in an open hand. The bell holds the time.
Desire. In the handbook, a want that promises to get. For a beginner, Epictetus says: set it down for now, and choose lightly instead. Today's word.
Your line: gently, for now. Pick one plan for today and attach the clause out loud or in your head: if nothing prevents me. Then go do it. Day three hundred thirty-four.

howItsDone: Some Stoic practitioners add a quiet reservation to their plans, such as 'if nothing prevents me', so they can act fully while holding the outcome lightly.

myth: Epictetus tells everyone to give up desire for the rest of their life
he says 'for the present': it's advice for someone just starting out.
he says to avoid only things that are in your own power
avoid sickness or death and you're bound to fall into what you avoid.
the Stoics attached a quiet reservation to their plans
something like: I'll go, if nothing prevents me.

fork.setup: you're new to the handbook and you badly want a promotion. what does section two suggest, for now?
options: want it with everything you've got.
set the desire down and choose your steps lightly.
fork.reveal: for a beginner, Epictetus says: set desire aside for now, and choose and refuse lightly, with a reservation.

original.note: Greek, Enchiridion 2: desire, a reaching out toward something.

trapdoor: what you thought: Stoics want nothing.
what it means: a beginner sets desire aside for now and chooses lightly, avoiding only what's in their own power.
what a scholar hears: Epictetus' three fields of training begin with desire and aversion; 'with reservation' renders a Stoic technical term, hupexairesis.

notes: Review (2026-10-01): 'disappointment is likely' changed to 'bound to be disappointed' to match the text's necessity; 'a clause attached to every plan' (absolute, and the market example is not in Enchiridion 2) replaced by Seneca's sailing example, now cited; Discourses 3.2 added to sources for the trapdoor; a generalization about the listener softened.

Enchiridion 2 paraphrased throughout (desire and aversion's promises; move aversion to things in our power; take away desire 'for the present'; use only choosing and refusing, lightly, with reservation).

The market example of a reservation is a standard illustration in modern discussions (Seneca, On Tranquility 13, uses a similar formula); it is not in Enchiridion 2 itself. Confirm phrasing 'The Stoics meant…'.
Greek ὄρεξις, and hupexairesis (ὑπεξαίρεσις) as the term behind 'with reservation': confirm.
Epictetus' three fields of study (desire/aversion, impulse/duty, assent) are set out in Discourses 3.2; confirm the trapdoor wording.
Neighbors (in sha Allah; James 4:15) mentioned briefly and without comparison.
